result: A conditional Mad2l1 knockout mouse model was successfully generated with efficient recombination in T cells and hepatocytes. LoxP sites flanking exons 2-5 of Mad2l1 were inserted, and Cre-mediated recombination resulted in deletion of ~90% of the Mad2l1 ORF in both T cells (via Lck-Cre) and hepatocytes (via Alb-Cre).
evaluation: Claims C56-C62 describe the generation and validation of the conditional Mad2l1 knockout allele. The experimental design is clearly documented with supporting data from Southern blotting (C58) and PCR genotyping (C62) shown in Figure 1. The approach is standard for conditional knockout models and the validation data confirm successful targeting and efficient recombination.

result: Adult T cells can survive conditional inactivation of Mad2l1 in the absence of Trp53 mutations. Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice did not develop malignancies within the first year of life, and T cells developed normally, suggesting tolerance to Mad2l1 loss.
evaluation: Claims C6, C64-C66 are supported by survival data in Figure 1D showing no increased mortality in Mad2l1-deleted T cells with wild-type Trp53. The observation that T cells develop normally provides functional evidence for tolerance. This is a key finding that contrasts with germline lethality of Mad2l1 deletion.

result: Loss of Mad2l1 and Trp53 in T cells causes rapidly lethal T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). On a Trp53-heterozygous background, ~50% of animals died by ~8 months, while on a Trp53-homozygous deletion background, half died by ~4 months. Double mutants showed statistically significant acceleration compared to Trp53 deletion alone.
evaluation: Claims C8, C50, C67, C69, C70, C78, C79, C213 are strongly supported by survival curves in Figure 1D with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.01). The synergistic effect of Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss is clearly demonstrated. The rapid kinetics and high penetrance provide robust evidence for the oncogenic cooperation.

result: Mad2l1-mutant animals exhibited dyspnea consistent with thymic hypertrophy. Post-mortem analysis revealed ~10-15 fold increase in thymus mass and 70% increase in spleen mass. Histological analysis showed rapidly dividing blasts with irregular nuclei consistent with lymphoma.
evaluation: Claims C72-C77 are supported by quantitative measurements (Figure 1F) and histological images (Figure 1G). The clinical observations, gross pathology, and microscopic features are internally consistent and characteristic of T-ALL. The evidence is descriptive but well-documented.

result: FACS analysis of thymi from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals revealed numerous dividing and undifferentiated blasting cells. The phenotype was fully penetrant, with even macroscopically normal thymi showing abnormal cells. Blasting cells were present in spleen but not peripheral blood, consistent with T-ALL.
evaluation: Claims C80-C87 are supported by FACS data in Figure 1H showing clear differences between mutant and control animals. The full penetrance claim is supported by observation in ~10% of animals with normal-appearing thymi. The pattern of organ involvement is consistent with T-ALL biology.

result: T-ALLs from Mad2l1-deleted mice were clonal based on TCR rearrangement analysis. Array-based CGH analysis revealed a single dominant rearranged TCR in each animal, indicating tumors arose from a single checkpoint-null initiating cell that underwent extensive proliferation.
evaluation: Claims C88-C91 are supported by aCGH data of TCR loci (Figure 1—figure supplement 2). The clonality evidence is strong and the inference that tumors arise from single cells following many divisions (C91) is reasonable given the macroscopic tumor size and clonal TCR rearrangements.

result: Adult hepatocytes can survive conditional inactivation of Mad2l1. Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice had normal lifespan, but double mutants with Trp53 deletion died significantly younger. Liver-specific Trp53 deletion alone had no impact on lifespan, consistent with Trp53 being only mildly oncogenic in hepatocytes.
evaluation: Claims C7, C92-C95 are supported by survival data in Figure 2A with appropriate statistical analysis. The differential effects of Trp53 deletion in liver versus thymus are well-documented and consistent with tissue-specific tumor suppressor functions. The comparison to previous literature (C95) strengthens the interpretation.

result: Conditional inactivation of Mad2l1 in hepatocytes causes progressive development of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Mice exhibited a characteristic progression from regeneration nodules (~4 months) to hepatocellular adenoma (HCA, >50% by 8-12 months) to HCC (50% by 12-16 months). Tumors were often large and invasive.
evaluation: Claims C9, C51, C96-C98, C100, C102, C103, C176, C214 are supported by histological analysis at multiple time points (Figure 2C, 2D) and gross pathology (Figure 2B). The progressive nature of disease and high penetrance are well-documented. The temporal progression provides strong evidence for a multi-step carcinogenesis process.

result: Deletion of Trp53 dramatically accelerated HCC onset in Mad2l1-deleted hepatocytes. In Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals, 75% of 8-12 month old animals exhibited HCC, occasionally in combination with HCA or cholangiocarcinoma.
evaluation: Claims C104-C106, C113 are supported by incidence data in Figure 2D and Table 1. The acceleration is dramatic and statistically significant. The data clearly demonstrate synergy between Mad2l1 and Trp53 loss in hepatocytes, paralleling findings in T cells.

result: Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53R246S mice (carrying the murine analog of the human Trp53-R249S mutation) experienced early death and extensive HCC, recapitulating a known feature of human disease.
evaluation: Claims C110, C111, C114 are supported by survival data in Figure 2E showing accelerated mortality compared to controls (p<0.001). The use of a clinically relevant Trp53 mutation strengthens the translational relevance of the model. The comparison to human disease is appropriate given the mutation's prevalence in human HCC.

result: Longitudinal MRI imaging revealed that HCC tumors in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals grew exponentially with an average doubling time of ~28 days. The number of tumors increased with age, averaging 3 morphologically distinct tumors per animal by 12 months, indicating progressive multi-focal cancer.
evaluation: Claims C115-C121, C215 are supported by MRI measurements (Figure 2F-H) with validation by histology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The exponential growth kinetics are well-characterized with quantitative data from 32 tumors across 9 animals. The multi-focal nature is clearly documented. The doubling time is rapid for solid tumors, supporting the aggressive nature of these cancers.

result: Mad2l1 DNA, mRNA, and protein were below detection levels in virtually all T-ALLs from Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53f/f animals (except tumor 33 with incomplete switching). In HCCs, both recombined and unrecombined Mad2l1 alleles were detected, with some HCCs showing high recombination efficiency suggesting most or all transformed hepatocytes lack functional Mad2l1.
evaluation: Claims C127-C130, C135-C136 are supported by multiple orthogonal methods: genomic PCR, aCGH, qPCR, and Western blotting (Figure 3). The differential recombination efficiency between T-ALLs and HCCs is well-explained by tissue composition and tumor invasiveness (C131-C132). The conclusion that some HCCs have high recombination is appropriately cautious given the mixed cell populations.

result: Mad2l1-null MEFs generated by Dox-inducible Cre showed efficient Mad2l1 excision and could be passaged multiple times. Wild-type MEFs exposed to nocodazole showed ~20-fold increase in mitotic index reflecting checkpoint-mediated arrest, while Mad2l1Δ/Δ MEFs showed only modest increase, consistent with loss of SAC-mediated mitotic delay.
evaluation: Claims C137-C142 are supported by PCR, Western blotting (Figure 4A), and phospho-H3 staining (Figure 4B) with time-lapse imaging (Video 1). The functional assay clearly demonstrates loss of checkpoint function in Mad2l1-deleted cells. The ability to passage Mad2l1-null MEFs multiple times is important evidence that SAC loss is compatible with cell survival in culture.

result: In vivo paclitaxel treatment increased phospho-H3 positive CD4+CD8+ thymocytes 6-fold in wild-type mice but only 2.5-fold in Lck-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ mice, demonstrating functional impairment of the mitotic checkpoint in Mad2l1Δ/Δ thymocytes in vivo. This confirms that loss of SAC function is compatible with rapid growth of both liquid and solid tumors.
evaluation: Claims C143-C146 are supported by phospho-H3 staining data (Figure 4C). The in vivo functional assay provides important validation that checkpoint loss persists in the tissue context. The reduced but not absent response to paclitaxel is noted by the authors as potentially reflecting mixed cell populations or partial SAC function, which is an appropriate caveat.

result: T-ALLs had a median of 3 whole chromosome alterations per tumor while HCCs had a median of 2. Loss of Chr13 and gain of Chr15 were frequent in both tumor types. Tissue-specific patterns were observed: T-ALLs gained Chr4 and Chr12 while HCCs lost these chromosomes (p<0.001, p<0.01); Chr18 showed preferential gain in HCCs but loss in T-ALLs (p<0.001).
evaluation: Claims C147-C154 are supported by aCGH data (Figure 5A-C) with appropriate statistical analysis. The tissue-specific patterns are clearly demonstrated and statistically significant. This is a key finding showing that while CIN occurs in both tumor types, the selective pressures differ by tissue. The statistical tests are appropriate for the comparisons made.

result: Chromosome ploidy correlated significantly with mRNA expression levels of genes on those chromosomes in both tumor types. However, differentially expressed genes were not the same between HCC and T-ALL, even for Chr15 which was gained in both. This indicates tissue-specific patterns of chromosome alterations likely due to tissue-specific gene expression changes.
evaluation: Claims C155-C157, C160-C163 are supported by correlation analysis (Figure 5D-E) and expression data (Figure 5F-G). The correlation between ploidy and expression demonstrates gene dosage effects. The tissue-specific differential expression despite similar ploidy changes is a sophisticated observation suggesting complex selective pressures. The inference about tissue-specific selection (C162) is reasonable but appropriately presented as speculation.

result: Recurrent focal CNVs included known cancer genes: ~30% of T-ALLs carried deletions spanning Pten (a negative regulator of PI3 kinase), and 5-10% of HCCs carried amplifications in Met (a known oncogene in human HCC), with confirmed Met RNA and protein overexpression.
evaluation: Claims C164-C168 are supported by aCGH data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-B) with validation by qPCR and Western blotting (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D). The identification of known cancer genes provides important validation that the CIN-driven alterations are under selection. The functional validation of Met overexpression strengthens the conclusion.

result: Focal CNVs were more frequent in T-ALL than HCC: T-ALLs carried a median of 29 CNVs per tumor with average size of ~40 genes per CNV, whereas HCCs carried ~20 CNVs per tumor with average size of ~2-3 genes (both differences statistically significant, p<0.05 and p<0.01).
evaluation: Claims C171-C173 are supported by quantitative analysis (Figure 5I-J) with statistical testing. However, the authors appropriately note a significant caveat (C174-C175): T-ALLs are clonal while HCCs are likely polyclonal, which could affect CNV assessment by aCGH. The authors acknowledge that single-cell methods would be needed to confirm this observation. The statistical significance is reported but the biological interpretation remains uncertain due to this confounding factor.

result: Chromosomes 15, 16, and 18 were frequently gained in both HCC and HCA, though signals were weaker in HCA suggesting only a subset of cells had undergone chromosome gain. Overall, HCA appeared more aneuploid than normal tissue, and HCC more aneuploid than HCA.
evaluation: Claims C177-C180 are supported by aCGH data (Figure 6A-B) with quantitative analysis. The progressive increase in aneuploidy from normal to HCA to HCC is consistent with a multi-step progression model. The inference about subset of cells in HCA (C178) is reasonable based on the weaker aCGH signals.

result: CNV similarity analysis using Jaccard Index revealed that two pairs of HCA and HCC tumors were strongly related, and two HCCs from the same mouse were strongly related. However, in three animals HCA and HCCs were weakly related, and in four animals no significant similarity was detected. Only 10-20% of CNVs overlapped between benign and malignant tumors from the same animal, suggesting HCC can evolve from HCA but HCA may not be a necessary precursor.
evaluation: Claims C181-C188 are supported by Jaccard Index analysis (Table 2) with appropriate statistical thresholds (Z-score >1.96). The mixed results showing some related and some unrelated tumor pairs support the nuanced conclusion that HCA can but need not be a precursor to HCC. The low CNV overlap even in related tumors suggests ongoing genomic instability. The conclusions are appropriately cautious.

result: Progression from HCA to HCC and clonal evolution are accompanied by ongoing gain and loss of whole chromosomes and CNVs.
evaluation: Claim C189 is supported by the CNV analysis of related tumors showing both shared and unique alterations. The low overlap of CNVs (10-20%) even in related tumors, combined with the progressive increase in aneuploidy, provides strong evidence for ongoing CIN during tumor evolution.

result: Single-cell sequencing revealed no chromosomal abnormalities in wild-type T cells but extensive aneuploidy in three T-ALL samples. Most cells from all three T-ALLs had gained Chr14 and Chr15, but changes in other chromosomes appeared random with >70% of cells having unique karyotypes. Heterogeneity scores were higher than in T-ALLs with truncated Mps1.
evaluation: Claims C190-C197, C235 are supported by single-cell sequencing data (Figure 6C-F) and heterogeneity score analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). The extensive intratumor heterogeneity is striking and provides direct evidence for ongoing CIN. The comparison to Mps1-truncated T-ALLs (C197) suggests complete SAC loss causes more severe CIN than partial inactivation. The single-cell approach is the gold standard for assessing heterogeneity.

result: Because T-ALLs were clonal based on TCR loci, the most likely explanation for intratumor karyotypic heterogeneity is ongoing chromosome loss and gain, presumably due to loss of SAC function.
evaluation: Claims C198-C200 integrate TCR clonality data (C88-C89) with single-cell karyotype heterogeneity (C191-C195). The logic is sound: clonal origin combined with extensive karyotypic diversity implies ongoing instability rather than polyclonal origin. The attribution to SAC loss (C200) is reasonable given the known function of Mad2l1, though the inference is appropriately presented as presumptive.

result: Comparison to human TCGA data revealed that human HCCs commonly gain Chr1q and Chr8q and lose Chr8p (associated with worse outcomes). Human Chr8q is syntenic to murine Chr15, which is frequently gained in Mad2l1-null HCCs. Similar patterns are found in HCC and breast cancer (consistent with pan-cancer karyotype), but non-epithelial cancers show very different patterns, suggesting different selective pressures.
evaluation: Claims C203-C212 are supported by TCGA data analysis (Figure 7) and synteny information from cited literature. The comparison between mouse and human tumors strengthens the translational relevance of the model. The observation of tissue-type-specific patterns (epithelial vs non-epithelial) parallels the findings in the mouse model. The speculation about different selective pressures (C212) is reasonable but appropriately tentative.

result: Trp53 mutations promote oncogenesis and substantially accelerate tumor development in Mad2l1-deleted backgrounds. Both T cells and hepatocytes survive checkpoint loss in the presence or absence of Trp53 mutation, but the combination accelerates disease onset in animals already mutant for a potent tumor suppressor.
evaluation: Claims C47-C49, C63, C216, C224-C225 are supported by survival data comparing different genotypes (Figures 1D, 2A) and citations to previous work. The synergistic effects are clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistics. The observation that cells can survive Mad2l1 loss even without Trp53 mutation (C48-C49) but that Trp53 loss accelerates tumorigenesis is an important finding about the relationship between checkpoint loss and tumor suppressor inactivation.

result: Mad2l1 deletion in hepatocytes is sufficient to cause HCC without Trp53 deletion, showing that Trp53 deletion is not a prerequisite for tumorigenesis. Loss of Mad2l1 in adult tissues can be strongly oncogenic, in contrast to heterozygous Mad2l1 deletion which is only weakly cancer promoting.
evaluation: Claims C112, C217-C218, C220 are supported by tumor incidence data in Alb-Cre::Mad2l1f/f::Trp53+/+ animals (Figure 2C-D, Table 1) and comparison to heterozygous animals. The observation that complete Mad2l1 loss is strongly oncogenic while heterozygous loss is weak (C220, C221) is important for understanding dosage effects and is supported by comparison to previous literature.

result: SAC inactivation is compatible with proliferation of some cell types but not others. Previous work showed checkpoint deficiency is tolerated by basal epidermal skin cells but lethal to hair follicle stem cells. Since most T-ALLs are clonal and lack Mad2l1 expression, they must arise from a single checkpoint-null initiating cell following many rounds of cell division.
evaluation: Claims C43-C44, C227-C230 integrate findings from the current study with previous work (C227 supported by citation). The inference that SAC requirements differ by cell type is well-supported. The conclusion that T-ALLs arise from single checkpoint-null cells after extensive proliferation (C229-C230) is strongly supported by the combination of clonality data and macroscopic tumor size.

result: Loss of Mad2l1 creates a mutator phenotype in the absence of an overt oncogenic driver. Large-scale genomic analysis of Mad2l1-deficient tumors may be useful for identifying new oncogenes and tumor suppressors. Mad2l1f/f animals may be useful for studying genomic instability in drug resistance and tumor recurrence.
evaluation: Claim C232 is supported by the extensive genomic alterations documented throughout the manuscript. Claims C233-C234 are speculative statements about future utility of the model, appropriately presented as such. The speculation is reasonable given the demonstrated mutator phenotype and the identification of known cancer genes (Pten, Met) in the current study.

result: Pathway analysis revealed that the only common pathways affected in T-ALLs and HCC were metabolic pathways, in agreement with previous findings that aneuploidy disrupts metabolism in multiple organisms.
evaluation: Claims C158-C159 are supported by Webgestalt pathway analysis and citations to previous work. The finding that metabolic pathways are commonly affected despite tissue-specific chromosome alterations suggests a general consequence of aneuploidy. The agreement with previous literature strengthens the conclusion.

result: Background and context claims about aneuploidy, CIN, and cancer biology from the introduction, including the burden of aneuploidy on normal cells, prevalence of abnormal karyotypes in tumors, models of genome restabilization, and tumor heterogeneity.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C14-C31 are background knowledge claims from the introduction, supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These provide context for the experimental work but are not novel findings of this study. The citations appear appropriate for the claims made.

result: Background claims about mouse models of CIN, SAC function, and previous work on Mad2l1 deletion in different cell types, including that germline SAC deletion is lethal and that Mad2l1 deletion is tolerated by interfollicular epidermal cells but not hair follicle stem cells.
evaluation: Claims C32-C42 are background knowledge and citations to previous work, including the authors' own prior studies. These establish the rationale for the current study and are appropriately supported by citations. The claims about SAC function (C34-C35) are well-established in the field.

result: Methodological and contextual claims about the experimental approach, including that CIN can be induced by inactivating SAC, germline inactivation is lethal, cancers require many cell divisions, Trp53 mutations were introduced to tolerize cells, hepatocytes are normally polyploid, and the Mad2l1f/f mice represent a valuable tool.
evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C45-C46, C61, C222 are methodological rationale and established knowledge. These are appropriately supported by the experimental design and citations. Claim C222 about the model being a valuable tool is a reasonable conclusion given the demonstrated utility in the manuscript.

result: T-ALL and HCC resulting from Mad2l1 deletion are lethal diseases. The liver cancer model resembles human HCC, which is also multi-focal and progressive.
evaluation: Claims C10 and C122 are supported by survival data showing mortality in tumor-bearing animals and comparison to human disease characteristics. The lethality is clearly demonstrated, and the comparison to human HCC is appropriate given the multi-focal progressive nature documented by MRI.

result: The rapid growth of Mad2l1-deficient tumors is surprising given previous data showing Mad2l1 is essential for cancer cell line survival and early embryo development, and that RNAi-mediated depletion causes mitotic catastrophe within six cell doublings.
evaluation: Claims C123-C126, C223 appropriately contextualize the findings relative to previous work (supported by citations). The surprise expressed (C124) is justified given the contrast with prior studies. This highlights the novelty and importance of the finding that adult tissues can tolerate complete Mad2l1 loss.

result: Speculation that hepatocytes may be more tolerant of chromosome number changes due to normal polyploidy, and that consequences of Mad2l1 inactivation for chromosome structure differ by cell type with fewer and smaller CNV lesions in HCC than T-ALL.
evaluation: Claim C219 is speculation (appropriately presented as such) about why hepatocytes tolerate Mad2l1 loss. Claim C231 about differential CNV characteristics is supported by data (Figure 5I-J) but the authors note the caveat about clonality differences (C174-C175) that could affect interpretation. The speculation is reasonable but requires further validation.

result: The near-complete absence of response to nocodazole in Mad2l1-deleted MEFs is consistent with checkpoint inactivation, though in vivo experiments with thymocytes reveal partial responsiveness to taxol.
evaluation: Claim C226 is supported by the functional assay data (Figure 4B-C). The authors appropriately note the discrepancy between complete loss in MEFs and partial response in thymocytes, acknowledging uncertainty about whether this reflects mixed cell populations or partial SAC function. This honest assessment of ambiguity is appropriate.

result: In some animals with liver cancer, there was evidence of clonal progression from HCA to HCC and genetic progression among physically distinct HCCs in a single animal. This is consistent with findings from ultra-deep sequencing of lung cancers showing extensive intra-tumor heterogeneity.
evaluation: Claims C236-C238 are supported by CNV similarity analysis (Table 2) and comparison to published literature. The evidence for clonal progression in some but not all cases is appropriately nuanced. The comparison to lung cancer studies strengthens the generalizability of the findings.

result: The average karyotype of Mad2l1-deficient tumor populations shows pan-cancer and tissue-specific patterns of chromosome alterations. Karyotypic variation causes differential loss/gain of cancer genes and large-scale gene expression changes. Selection in the face of ongoing CIN contrasts with genome restabilization models where CIN is transient.
evaluation: Claims C239, C241-C243, C245 are supported by aCGH and expression data throughout the manuscript. Claim C244 about selection at multiple levels is speculation but reasonable given the data. The contrast with genome restabilization models (C245) is an important conceptual contribution, though the authors appropriately note that further experiments would be needed to definitively distinguish between models.
